Small-scale implementation under actual operating conditions before full rollout. A pilot validates effect and side effects with real operators before scaling; define measurable exit criteria and a rollback plan.

Models process behavior virtually to compare scenarios without live disruption. Useful when live experiments are risky or expensive; results depend on realistic inputs and validated model assumptions.

Weights criteria such as risk, impact, and cost to choose among solutions. Use when several solutions offer different benefits, costs, and risks; score against agreed criteria rather than intuition alone.
Lists rollout tasks, owners, timing, training, resources, and risks. Connect owners, deadlines, training, contingency actions, and metrics so gains persist after the project team leaves.

Pugh matrix compares each option against a baseline: (1) + better; (2) S/= same; (3) − worse. Combine strong features where possible. Use early in concept selection when exact costs/performance are uncertain; the datum helps reveal trade-offs and hybrid designs.

SPC (Statistical Process Control): Use statistical charts to distinguish common- from special-cause variation. Developed from Walter Shewhart's control-chart work; SPC detects process instability before judging capability to meet specs.
Inherent routine variation present when a process is statistically stable. A stable process still has common-cause variation; reduce it by changing the underlying system, not chasing every point.

Unusual identifiable variation outside the process's routine behavior. Investigate an assignable cause and contain potential defects before changing settings; not every nonconforming unit is a special-cause signal.

Unnecessary adjustment to common-cause fluctuation that increases variability. Deming's funnel experiment illustrates why adjusting a stable process after every ordinary fluctuation can make results worse.
Time-series chart with centerline and statistically derived control limits. Control limits describe process behavior, unlike customer-set specifications; charts answer stability, not capability.

Control-chart zones, on each side of centerline: (1) Zone C: 0–1σ; (2) Zone B: 1–2σ; (3) Zone A: 2–3σ. Used in run rules. Zone rules detect nonrandom patterns inside the 3σ limits; apply the predefined rule set consistently to avoid excessive false alarms.

terms.term: Selection of variables for control charting
terms.def: Prioritize critical inputs and outputs tied to customer needs for chart monitoring. Monitor outputs that customers care about and upstream inputs that operators can control; avoid charting every available metric.

Group close-in-time observations to expose between-group special causes. Form subgroups close enough in time that common short-term conditions are shared; process changes should appear between groups.

X̄–R chart = X-bar (subgroup mean) and R (subgroup range) charts; for small rational subgroups, often n = 2–10. Use X-bar for mean changes and R for within-subgroup dispersion with small rational subgroups; interpret the R chart first.

X̄–s chart = X-bar (subgroup mean) and s (subgroup standard deviation) charts; useful for larger subgroups. Use when subgroup size is large enough that the standard deviation is a more informative spread estimate than the range.

ImR (Individuals and Moving Range) charts track (1) individual observations and (2) successive moving ranges when subgroup size = 1. Use ImR for one reading per interval, e.g., daily batch yield; serial correlation can undermine standard control limits.

p chart: Tracks p = proportion of defective/nonconforming units; permits varying sample sizes by adjusting control limits. Use for fraction of defective units in subgroup samples; varying n produces different UCL/LCL values.

np chart: Tracks np = number of defective/nonconforming units; requires a constant subgroup size n. Use when samples all have the same n and the intuitive metric is number of defective units, not percentage defective.

c chart: Tracks c = count of defects/nonconformities when opportunity or inspection area is constant. Use for defects per constant inspection unit, e.g., scratches on the same area; multiple defects on one unit are counted separately.

u chart: Tracks u = defects per unit when the inspected opportunity, area, or number of units varies. Use when opportunity varies, e.g., defects per document across documents of different lengths; adjust limits for inspected size.

Short-run SPC (Statistical Process Control): Uses standardized or target-deviation charts across small-lot part families. For low-volume/high-mix products, standardize across similar part families or chart deviations from individual targets.

DNOM (Deviation from Nominal) chart: Plots each result minus its part-specific target for short-run SPC (Statistical Process Control). Use when products have different nominal values but comparable deviations; subtract each target to monitor shared process performance.

MAMR (Moving Average and Moving Range) chart: Plots (1) rolling means and (2) moving ranges to monitor shifts while smoothing noise. A moving average smooths noise but can delay or mask abrupt shifts; do not interpret rolling observations as independent.

EWMA (Exponentially Weighted Moving Average) chart: Decreasing weight on older observations reveals sustained small shifts. Use EWMA for small, persistent mean shifts; its smoothing constant determines how rapidly past observations lose weight.

CUSUM (Cumulative Sum) chart: Running total of deviations from target identifies small persistent shifts. Use CUSUM when detecting small persistent deviations from target is more important than identifying only large single-point shifts.

Eight common SPC (Statistical Process Control) run rules: (1) 1 point beyond 3σ; (2) 9 on one side; (3) 6 trending; (4) 14 alternating; (5) 2 of 3 beyond 2σ same side; (6) 4 of 5 beyond 1σ same side; (7) 15 within 1σ; (8) 8 beyond 1σ, none in center. Each rule is a special-cause screening signal, not proof of a specific cause; different rule sets change the false-alarm rate.

Sustained increase or decrease over successive time points. Six monotonically increasing or decreasing points can trigger a run rule; investigate drift rather than correcting isolated common-cause noise.

Fifteen points near the centerline may signal artificial suppression of variation. Points unnaturally clustered at the center can imply stratification or mixing/smoothing of subgroup data; check collection practice.
Eight points avoiding the center zone may indicate mixed distributions. Points avoiding the centerline may indicate alternating processes or mixed sources; investigate how samples were subgrouped.

TPM (Total Productive Maintenance): Operator-involved equipment care to improve reliability and OEE (Overall Equipment Effectiveness). Use operator inspections and planned equipment care to remove minor stops and unplanned failures; track impact through OEE.

Maintenance strategies: (1) Preventive/time-based; (2) Condition-based; (3) Reliability-centered; (4) Predictive. Select by failure risk and data. Time-based maintenance prevents age-related failures; predictive maintenance uses condition signals to intervene before failure.

MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures): Operating time between successive failures of repairable equipment. Use MTBF for repairable assets' reliability, not nonrepairable lifetime; longer MTBF means failures occur less often.

MTTR (Mean Time to Repair): Average time needed to restore a failed item to service. Use MTTR for maintainability and restoration effectiveness; distinguish active repair time from broader downtime where needed.

Visual cues show expected condition and highlight process abnormalities immediately. Use real-time visual signals for abnormal conditions, production pace, safety, and standard work so issues are apparent without reports.
Visible or audible alert that calls attention to an abnormal condition. An andon alert supports immediate escalation and sometimes line stop to contain defects at their source.
Tool-storage board outlining each item's designated position. A 5S visual control: missing tools stand out immediately, reducing search time and improving accountability.
Recheck gage adequacy after process, instrument, or tolerance changes. Revalidate MSA if operators, software, measurement range, or process tolerances change; yesterday's GR&R may no longer apply.

Measurement uncertainty no greater than one-quarter of specification tolerance. A 4:1 test-uncertainty-to-tolerance screening guideline; consider decision risk and guard-banding rather than treating it as absolute.

Document specifying key controls, methods, limits, sampling, owners, and reaction steps. Use after Improve as the process owner's playbook: specify what to monitor, frequency, limits, escalation, and reaction actions.

Defined response, responsibility, and containment when a process signal occurs. Contain product and investigate causes after a genuine signal; avoid unauthorized adjustments that tamper with common-cause variation.

Formal transfer of improved process and monitoring to accountable operations owner. Include ownership, training, capability baselines, dashboards, and response rules before declaring DMAIC Control complete.
Record of project successes, mistakes, and reusable insights for future teams. Record failed hypotheses and implementation obstacles as well as successes so other teams avoid repeating them.
Transfer a proven improvement to other comparable processes or sites. Verify local customer needs, process similarity, and baseline before copying a successful change to another site.

SOP (Standard Operating Procedure): Controlled instructions to perform a process consistently. Use an SOP to lock in critical steps and document version-controlled training; periodically update it after improvement.
Onboarding teaches revised methods; refresher training prevents skill drift. Reinforce revised methods when personnel or conditions change; assess actual adherence, not just attendance records.
Continuously verify gains with process controls and performance measures. Track both outcome metrics and leading controls to detect regression early and return accountability to the process owner.

DFSS (Design for Six Sigma): Designs new or fundamentally revised products/processes to meet customer CTQs (Critical to Quality requirements) from the start. Use DFSS when no satisfactory process/design exists or when redesign is fundamental; validate requirements before launch.

DMADV (Design for Six Sigma roadmap): (1) (D) Define; (2) (M) Measure; (3) (A) Analyze; (4) (D) Design; (5) (V) Validate (sometimes Verify). Choose DMADV for a new or substantially redesigned offering; verify the resulting design with prototype, pilot, or user tests.

DMADOV (Design for Six Sigma roadmap): (1) (D) Define; (2) (M) Measure; (3) (A) Analyze; (4) (D) Design; (5) (O) Optimize; (6) (V) Validate (sometimes Verify). The extra Optimize stage explicitly tunes design settings/tolerances after initial design and before validation.

Verification checks specifications; validation checks real customer use and needs. Think 'built the design right' (verification) versus 'built the right design for users' (validation); both are required for DFSS.

DMAIC (Define–Measure–Analyze–Improve–Control) improves an existing process; DFSS (Design for Six Sigma) designs a new or fundamentally reworked process. Use DMAIC for chronic problems in a functioning process; use DFSS when requirements call for a fundamentally new design.

DFX (Design for X): Design with life-cycle objectives in mind; X may be (1) Cost; (2) Manufacturability; (3) Assembly; (4) Test; (5) Maintainability; (6) Service. Choose the relevant X early—for example, assembly time, testability, serviceability, or cost—before expensive design commitments.

DFC (Design for Cost): Design features and quality to meet a market-based target cost. Use target-cost thinking early in design, when architecture choices still control most downstream production cost.

LCC (Life Cycle Cost) includes (1) Purchase; (2) Shipping; (3) Installation; (4) Training; (5) Operation; (6) Support/maintenance; (7) Disposal, less any salvage value. Compare alternatives over acquisition, operating, maintenance, and disposal life; lowest purchase price may yield the highest LCC.

DFM/DFA = Design for Manufacturability / Design for Assembly. Ease production with (1) Fewer parts; (2) Standard parts; (3) Modular design; (4) Fewer fasteners; (5) Self-locating parts; (6) Achievable tolerances. Use DFM/DFA early to reduce assembly mistakes, part count, tooling, and manufacturing complexity; avoid tolerances tighter than function requires.

DFT (Design for Test): Build in access and features enabling easy inspection and functional testing. Build test points, diagnostics, and inspection access into the design; retrofitted testing is often costlier and less reliable.

Make maintenance safe, accessible, and fast with simple replacement and diagnostics. Design replaceable modules, safe access, and clear fault diagnostics to shorten service time and improve availability.

Deliver required functions at the lowest total cost without sacrificing performance. Assess required function divided by total cost; cost cutting that removes customer-required function is not value engineering.

Make design performance insensitive to uncontrolled noise and environmental variation. Taguchi-inspired robust design seeks target performance under changing noise conditions, not just average performance at ideal settings.
Allocate part tolerances to balance output performance against manufacturing cost. Tightening tolerances can raise manufacturing cost; allocate them where variation most affects final CTQs.

Assembly worst-case tolerance equals the sum of individual part tolerances. Use worst-case stack-up for must-fit safety-critical assemblies; it is conservative because all component extremes are assumed together.

For independent dimensions, combine variances by root-sum-of-squares. Root-sum-of-squares is useful for independent contributors to an assembly dimension; verify independence and distribution assumptions.
Quality loss rises as k(y−target)², even for results within specifications. Taguchi challenged the pass/fail view: even an in-spec deviation from target can cause economic or customer loss.

TRIZ (Russian acronym for Theory of Inventive Problem Solving): Resolve design contradictions using recurring inventive principles rather than accepting trade-offs. Developed by Genrich Altshuller from patterns in inventions; use TRIZ when design requirements conflict, such as strength versus weight.

glossary.Functional team: Team composed of members within the same department or specialty.
glossary.Projectized team: Dedicated members assigned to a project under a project manager.
glossary.Task force: Temporary team focused on a specific problem or mission.
glossary.Committee: Standing group with governance or review responsibilities.
glossary.Adjourning: The established team closes and disbands after finishing its work.
glossary.Reforming: A supposed team stage name; not a standard Tuckman stage.
glossary.Aligning: A plausible-sounding label, not a standard Tuckman stage.
glossary.Consultative style: A leader asks for input; this is not one of the four Blanchard style labels.
glossary.Transactional style: Leadership through contingent rewards and corrective exchanges.
glossary.Laissez-faire style: A hands-off leadership approach, not a named Blanchard situation style.
glossary.Absolute scale: A count-like measurement scale beyond the standard nominal–ratio classification.
glossary.Binary scale: A two-category coding, not a separate nominal–ratio scale.
glossary.Logarithmic scale: A transformed numeric scale, not one of the four classic measurement scales.
glossary.Transportation waste: Unnecessary movement of products or materials between locations.
glossary.Inventory waste: Excess stock or work awaiting downstream demand.
glossary.Waiting waste: Idle time while people, materials, or information await the next step.
glossary.Motion waste: Unnecessary movement of people, such as walking to retrieve supplies.
glossary.Defects waste: Scrap or rework arising from items that fail requirements.
glossary.Overproduction waste: Making more or earlier than the next operation needs.
glossary.Overprocessing waste: Extra work beyond what the customer requires.
